Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The economic downturn may take its toll at the 2009 Cannes Film Festival, which opens Wednesday night. But as always, the show will go on. Eli Roth and Brad Pitt are men on a mission in Quentin Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds." Studios are cutting back on parties and all the glitz that goes with them, according to news reports. Moreover, there will be fewer people around to cover Cannes, as news organizations around the world trim costs. (Several, in fact, have tightened up by eliminating their movie reviewers.) Nevertheless, those who attend may see a bumper crop of good and intriguing films, Variety's Jay Weissberg told Reuters. "We've all been hoping Cannes would pull something out of the bag to make us feel good again. On paper, they have." Leah Rozen, film critic for People magazine, said there are several promising contenders for the Palme d'Or, Cannes' top prize, as well as a number of notable movies premiering out of competition. "What Cannes really is, is an international festival, and you really see world cinema," she said. "This year, there are 52 films that are going to be represented, of which 20 are in competition."  See Rozen talk about some of this year's promising works » . Two of the films in competition are American: Quentin Tarantino's World War II movie, "Inglourious Basterds," and Ang Lee's "Taking Woodstock," a tale about the 1969 music festival. Tarantino told The New York Times that he's been hoping to do a war movie for years. "You've got to make a movie about something, and I'm a film guy, so I think in terms of genres," he said. However, the maker of "Pulp Fiction" and "Jackie Brown" added, that doesn't mean what he ends up with resembles what he started with: "It's simply the spark that starts the fire." "Inglourious Basterds" was inspired by a 1978 Italian film that starred Bo Svenson ("Walking Tall, Part 2") and football player-turned-actor Fred Williamson ("Black Caesar"). Tarantino's film, which he characterized to the Times as "not a remake," stars Brad Pitt and Mike Myers. Cannes has been good to Tarantino; he won the Palme d'Or for "Pulp Fiction" 15 years ago. Buzz has been high on "Basterds" since Tarantino announced the project several years ago. "Taking Woodstock," the new film by "Brokeback Mountain" director Lee, is based on the book by Elliot Tiber, whose hotelier parents owned a musical festival permit in Bethel, New York, where Woodstock was held. The cast includes Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton and Eugene Levy as Max Yasgur, on whose farm the festival was finally held. Other films in competition include Lars von Trier's "Antichrist," Jane Campion's "Bright Star" and Pedro Almodovar's "Broken Embraces."  Gallery: Some of Cannes' recent winners » . But this year's Cannes festival is attracting plenty of attention for its out-of-competition films as well. The festival is opening with "Up," the latest animated work from Pixar. "That sort of breaks convention to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon," Rozen said. Also at Cannes will be Heath Ledger's last film, "The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus." The Oscar-winning "Dark Knight" actor died during the making of the Terry Gilliam film; Gilliam managed to complete it by doing some rewriting and casting other actors -- including Jude Law, Colin Farrell and Johnny Depp -- to play Ledger's part. Despite the interest in seeing Ledger, the film is still struggling to find a buyer, though Entertainment Weekly recently reported that a Los Angeles screening went over well. Cannes, which also functions as a huge film marketplace, may widen the net in attracting distributors. But much of the fun from Cannes comes from the films that emerge from nowhere. Recent winners of the Palme d'Or include 2000's "Dancer in the Dark," which established singer Bjork as an actress, and "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days," a Romanian film that ended up topping many critics' lists in 2007. "One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments," Rozen said.

(CNN) -- The global economic downturn may cast a shadow over the 2009 Cannes Film Festival, which opens Wednesday evening, yet as always, the show will go on. Studios are reportedly scaling back on lavish parties and the customary glamour that accompanies them. Furthermore, fewer journalists will be on hand to cover the event, as news organizations worldwide continue to tighten their budgets—several, in fact, have gone so far as to eliminate their film critic positions entirely.

Nevertheless, those in attendance may be treated to an exceptional array of compelling and thought-provoking films this year. As Variety's Jay Weissberg told Reuters, "We've all been hoping Cannes would pull something out of the bag to make us feel good again. On paper, they have."

Leah Rozen, film critic for People magazine, noted that several strong contenders are vying for the Palme d'Or, Cannes' most prestigious honor, alongside numerous notable films premiering outside the main competition. "What Cannes really is, is an international festival, and you truly see world cinema," she explained. "This year, 52 films will be represented, 20 of which are in competition."

Among the competition entries are two American productions: Quentin Tarantino's World War II epic, "Inglourious Basterds," and Ang Lee's "Taking Woodstock," which chronicles the legendary 1969 music festival. Tarantino revealed to The New York Times that he had long harbored ambitions to direct a war film. "You've got to make a movie about something, and I'm a film guy, so I think in terms of genres," he said. Yet the director behind "Pulp Fiction" and "Jackie Brown" was quick to add that his finished work rarely mirrors his initial concept: "It's simply the spark that starts the fire."

"Inglourious Basterds" draws inspiration from a 1978 Italian film starring Bo Svenson ("Walking Tall, Part 2") and football-player-turned-actor Fred Williamson ("Black Caesar"). Tarantino's reimagining—which he was careful to describe to the Times as "not a remake"—features Brad Pitt and Mike Myers in leading roles. Cannes has historically favored Tarantino, who claimed the Palme d'Or for "Pulp Fiction" fifteen years ago, and anticipation for "Basterds" has been building ever since the project was first announced.

"Taking Woodstock," the latest offering from "Brokeback Mountain" director Ang Lee, is adapted from Elliot Tiber's memoir. Tiber's parents, as hoteliers, held the permit for the music festival ultimately staged in Bethel, New York. The film's ensemble cast includes Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton, and Eugene Levy, who portrays Max Yasgur, the farmer on whose land Woodstock was eventually held.

Other films competing for top honors include Lars von Trier's "Antichrist," Jane Campion's "Bright Star," and Pedro Almodóvar's "Broken Embraces."

This year's festival, however, is generating considerable buzz for its out-of-competition selections as well. Cannes will open with "Up," Pixar's latest animated feature. "That sort of breaks convention, to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon," Rozen observed.

Also screening will be Heath Ledger's final film, "The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus." The Oscar-winning "Dark Knight" star died during production of Terry Gilliam's film; Gilliam ultimately completed the project through creative rewrites, enlisting Jude Law, Colin Farrell, and Johnny Depp to share the role Ledger left unfinished. Despite considerable interest in seeing Ledger's final performance, the film has yet to secure a distributor, though Entertainment Weekly recently reported that a Los Angeles screening was well received. Cannes, which doubles as a major marketplace for film distribution, may help widen the pool of potential buyers.

Yet much of the festival's allure lies in the unexpected discoveries—films that emerge seemingly out of nowhere to capture attention. Recent Palme d'Or winners include 2000's "Dancer in the Dark," which established Björk as a formidable screen presence, and "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days," a Romanian production that topped numerous critics' year-end lists in 2007.

"One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments," Rozen reflected.

The global financial crisis is expected to cast a shadow over this year's Cannes Film Festival, kicking off Wednesday evening—yet the event will proceed as scheduled, as it always does. Adding to the leaner atmosphere, media coverage will likely shrink too, since news outlets worldwide are slashing budgets—some have even eliminated film critic positions entirely.

Despite these constraints, industry observers suggest attendees can still expect an impressive lineup of compelling films. Variety critic Jay Weissberg told Reuters that expectations were high for Cannes to deliver something uplifting this year, and initial indications suggest it has delivered.

People magazine film critic Leah Rozen noted several strong contenders vying for the prestigious Palme d'Or, alongside numerous noteworthy films screening outside the main competition. She emphasized that Cannes serves as a true showcase of international cinema, with 52 films representing the festival this year, 20 of which are competing for the top honor.

## American Entries Make Their Mark

The competition includes two American productions: Quentin Tarantino's WWII drama "Inglourious Basterds" and Ang Lee's "Taking Woodstock," which chronicles the legendary 1969 music gathering.

Speaking with The New York Times, Tarantino revealed he'd long wanted to tackle a war film, explaining his approach to filmmaking centers on genre. Yet he cautioned that his finished products often diverge significantly from their initial inspiration—the original concept merely ignites the creative process, he explained.

The film draws inspiration from a 1978 Italian production featuring Bo Svenson and Fred Williamson, though Tarantino insists his version isn't a remake. Brad Pitt and Mike Myers headline the cast. Cannes holds special significance for Tarantino, who claimed the Palme d'Or fifteen years ago for "Pulp Fiction," and anticipation for "Basterds" has been building since the project was first announced.

Meanwhile, "Taking Woodstock" adapts Elliot Tiber's memoir about his family's hotel business, which held the permit for the festival ultimately staged in Bethel, New York. The ensemble cast features Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton, and Eugene Levy portraying farm owner Max Yasgur.

Additional competition entries include Lars von Trier's "Antichrist," Jane Campion's "Bright Star," and Pedro Almodovar's "Broken Embraces."

## Beyond the Competition

This year's festival is also generating buzz for films screening outside the official competition. Pixar's animated feature "Up" opens the festival—an unconventional choice that Rozen noted breaks from tradition by launching with what is essentially a cartoon.

Also drawing attention is Heath Ledger's final performance in Terry Gilliam's "The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus." Following Ledger's death mid-production, Gilliam salvaged the project through creative rewrites, enlisting Jude Law, Colin Farrell, and Johnny Depp to collectively complete Ledger's role. Despite considerable curiosity surrounding the film, it remains without distribution, though a recent Los Angeles screening reportedly received a positive response according to Entertainment Weekly. Given that Cannes doubles as a major film marketplace, this exposure could help attract potential buyers.

## The Element of Surprise

Part of what makes Cannes exciting is discovering unexpected gems. Past Palme d'Or winners illustrate this unpredictability—2000's "Dancer in the Dark" launched Bjork's acting career, while the Romanian film "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days" went on to dominate critics' year-end lists in 2007.

Rozen observed that the festival consistently surprises her: films with modest expectations sometimes prove exceptional, while heavily anticipated releases can disappoint.

# Cannes Film Festival Opens Under Economic Cloud, But Star Power and Bold Cinema Persist

**CANNES, France** — The world's most glamorous film festival kicked off this week with a noticeably different atmosphere than in years past, as the global economic downturn cast a long shadow over the French Riviera's famed red carpet.

Industry insiders report that the Marché du Film, the festival's bustling film market, has seen a marked contraction in attendance and deal-making activity. Fewer independent distributors have made the trip this year, and several smaller production companies that once maintained a visible presence along the Croisette have scaled back or skipped the festival entirely. Hotel bookings reportedly dipped, and the flotilla of yachts lining the harbor appeared thinner than in boom years past.

"There's definitely a different energy this year," said one veteran sales agent who has attended the festival for over a decade. "The parties are smaller, budgets are tighter, but the films—the films are still extraordinary."

Despite the tightened purse strings, festival organizers pressed forward with a lineup considered one of the more daring in recent memory. Competition jury president Isabelle Huppert has presided over a slate of films tackling weighty themes, from war and trauma to family dysfunction and moral ambiguity.

Among the buzziest premieres has been Lars von Trier's psychological horror film "Antichrist," starring Willem Dafoe and Charlotte Gainsbourg, which reportedly left audiences gasping and, in some cases, walking out during its unflinching and graphic content. The film's press conference turned combative, with von Trier offering little apology for the visceral reactions his work provoked.

Quentin Tarantino returned to the festival with "Inglourious Basterds," his World War II revenge fantasy starring Brad Pitt, which drew one of the week's largest crowds and a lengthy standing ovation. The film's blend of violence, dark humor, and alternate history has already generated significant awards-season buzz.

Pixar's "Up" opened the festival as the first animated film to hold that honor, offering a rare note of family-friendly warmth amid otherwise heavy competition fare. Its 3D presentation and emotional storytelling earned praise from critics who called it a fitting, crowd-pleasing choice for the festival's opening night.

Other notable entries included Ang Lee's "Taking Woodstock," a lighter counterpoint exploring the famed 1969 music festival, and Jane Campion's "Bright Star," a romantic drama about poet John Keats that offered visual lushness amid the festival's darker offerings.

Despite the economic headwinds, festival director Thierry Frémaux insisted that Cannes remains committed to championing cinema as an art form, even—or especially—in difficult times.

"Cinema doesn't stop because the economy struggles," Frémaux said in remarks to reporters. "If anything, this is when we need these stories most."

Analysts note that the festival's ability to weather the downturn may serve as a bellwether for the broader film industry, which has faced declining DVD sales, tightened credit for independent financing, and studios' growing caution toward mid-budget films.

Still, longtime attendees say the spirit of Cannes—part artistic showcase, part marketplace, part spectacle—remains intact, even if the financial extravagance has been dialed back.

"The films this year have teeth," said one critic covering the festival for a European outlet. "Maybe that's what happens when the world gets harder. The stories get harder too."

The festival continues through the week, culminating in the awarding of the Palme d'Or, with predictions swirling around several of the competition's more provocative entries.

# Cannes 2009: Glamour Meets Grit as Recession Casts Shadow Over Croisette

**CANNES, France** — The world's most prestigious film festival opened this week under decidedly less extravagant circumstances than in years past, as the global financial crisis has left its mark on every red carpet, yacht party, and market stall along the famous Croisette.

## A More Sober Affair

Industry veterans note a palpable shift in atmosphere. Fewer mega-yachts crowd the harbor, hotel rates have softened for the first time in years, and studios have trimmed marketing budgets that once fueled the festival's legendary excess. Distributors arrived in Cannes this year with tighter checkbooks, and the traditionally frenzied film market has taken on a more cautious, deal-conscious tone. Buyers are pickier, financing is harder to secure, and mid-budget films are struggling to find the kind of bidding wars that once defined Cannes.

Yet despite the economic gloom, the festival's programming suggests audiences—and filmmakers—are hungry for both escapism and reflection.

## Pixar's "Up" Provides a Lift

In a historic first, Pixar's "Up" opened the festival, marking the first animated film and first 3D film to do so in Cannes' 62-year history. The heartfelt story of an elderly widower who ties thousands of balloons to his house resonated as a symbol of resilience and reinvention—themes not lost on a festival grappling with economic uncertainty. Critics praised the film's emotional depth, and its selection signaled that even in lean times, audiences crave stories of hope and adventure.

## Ang Lee's "Taking Woodstock" Revisits Another Turbulent Era

Ang Lee's "Taking Woodstock," based on Elliot Tiber's memoir about the events leading up to the 1969 festival, offered a nostalgic yet pointed parallel. The film's depiction of a generation seeking transcendence amid social and economic upheaval felt timely to festival-goers drawing comparisons between countercultural disillusionment then and financial anxiety now. Lee's gentler, comedic approach—a departure from his more intense recent work—was seen by some as a deliberate tonal choice, offering audiences relief rather than confrontation.

## Terry Gilliam's Troubled Triumph

Perhaps no film embodied the festival's undercurrents of crisis and survival more than Terry Gilliam's **"The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus."** The fantasy film, notoriously completed after star Heath Ledger's death during production, became a symbol of art persevering through hardship. The film's premiere was as emotional as it was celebratory, with Gilliam speaking candidly about the challenges of financing and completing the project—challenges that mirrored the broader industry's current struggles to get films made and distributed in a tightening market.

## An Industry at a Crossroads

Trade analysts covering the market noted that fewer high-priced deals were changing hands this year, with buyers focusing on films with modest budgets and clearer commercial paths. Some sales agents described a "wait and see" approach among distributors reluctant to commit to big numbers amid box office uncertainty at home.

Still, festival director Thierry Frémaux maintained that Cannes' cultural mission remained unchanged. "Cinema doesn't stop because of economic difficulty," he said in press remarks. "If anything, it becomes more necessary."

Whether that necessity translates into ticket sales and distribution deals remains to be seen. But as the lights dimmed for opening night, one thing was clear: even in a recession, Cannes still knows how to put on a show—just with a bit less confetti than usual.
